name: Cloud Computing

claims.claim_text: A product whose function depends on a vendor-operated service inherits that vendor's lifespan: the service is unlikely to survive ten years and will almost certainly not survive twenty, at which point the hardware simply stops working.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's cloud-based, right, it relies on a service on the Internet to work, right, be it cloud or whatever it is, right, it relies on the company
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The standard defence against tool obsolescence — keeping the old CAD package or compiler alive on a preserved machine — has no equivalent when the processing happens on the vendor's servers, so a hosted tool cannot be archived alongside the design it produced.
claims.quote_verbatim: not like you can keep this program running for the next 10 years because you've invested
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Google Glass & Adafruit - Obtaining Ostentatious Oculiforms

claims.claim_text: The test for whether a browser-based tool is genuinely a hosted service is whether it needs live internet access while you work: if the application and the file can be kept locally and run offline, it is a desktop application that happens to render in a browser, and it carries none of the dependency risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: does it need access to the internet live while you're laying out that board or not
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Hosted design tools have produced multi-week lockouts in practice — one user reported being unable to export schematics for over eighteen days with no support response — and during such an outage the work is neither editable nor retrievable.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can't export schematics, uh, for over 18 days now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Running a design tool online creates two dependencies at once — your connection and the provider's infrastructure — and the model works at the scale of a major mail provider while smaller companies lack the resources to make it equally robust.
claims.quote_verbatim: you are 100% reliant on, A, your internet connection, and B, their server being up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Anything hosted, including your own site and documentation, can disappear, so material worth keeping needs to be both archived and spread across enough independent copies that no single service's failure removes it.
claims.quote_verbatim: running your own site your own documentation anything like that can go away
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Open Circuits with Eric Schlaepfer and Windell Oskay

claims.claim_text: A decision that concerns only local state should be made locally; sending the data out, processing it remotely and sending the result back adds layers without adding capability. Remote monitoring of that same system is a separate and legitimate feature.
claims.quote_verbatim: you, if you want to do something locally, you do it locally. You don't spit it out to the internet of things cloud and then do the processing in the cloud and then spit it back to your device
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: Edge processing means the device does the interpretation and sends events rather than raw data upward, leaving aggregation as the remote system's job — which collapses both bandwidth and storage cost against streaming everything.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the, the processing happens in the box and, uh, we are sending, um, uh, what we, what basically what we call events up to the cloud
claims.speaker: Joe Bamberg

claims.claim_text: The opposite split is equally defensible when the algorithm is complex and changes often: reduce the sensor data just enough on device, run the real algorithm remotely, and firmware becomes dramatically simpler while the analysis can be re-run over the same recorded dataset as many times as needed instead of going through a download-test-wait cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: get it up to the cloud because computing is nearly free so that all the fermentation algorithms are in the cloud and it makes firmware so much easier
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: Users do not want sensor readings, they want the conclusion drawn from them, which is what determines where the interpretation layer has to live rather than any principle about edges and centres.
claims.quote_verbatim: no one cares about like the sensor. They want to know like information
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: A voice-controlled device runs a wake-word detector locally, then sends the request to a remote service which in turn commands the target device, so a single spoken command traverses the internet twice before a light changes state.
claims.quote_verbatim: listening for the trigger word
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Keeping voice processing on a local network buys response time and removes the internet dependency, but a model that fits on the device will not match one trained against a far larger corpus — the trade is accuracy against latency and autonomy, not a free win.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to get some kind of like neuro-linguistic processing NLP unit on board, it's not going to be as good as something that's trained against lots and lots of different words
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Local voice processing is viable but hardware-bound: on an older single-board computer a response can take around ten seconds, where routing the same request to a hosted service returns essentially instantly — which is the real reason people give up local processing.
claims.quote_verbatim: on like a CM4 of, you know, especially a pie, if it's an older pie, like something probably like pie three, for example, it might take 10 seconds to respond
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: Offloading the heavy processing keeps the on-device application small, which is why speech recognition historically shipped an audio file to a server rather than carrying the model.
claims.quote_verbatim: it could, the app could be much smaller if all the processing is offline
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Worktrips and Workspaces - Junket Jactation Jiltedness

claims.claim_text: The durable division of labour for machine learning on small devices is to train remotely and infer locally: hosted tooling consumes labelled sensor data and emits inference models sized to run on a resource-constrained microcontroller, so the developer never has to be a data scientist.
claims.quote_verbatim: takes labeled sensor data and it generates all these inferencing models that you could then run on device in a resource constrained microcontroller
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Cheap compute and ubiquitous connectivity make it possible to put a radio on anything, and the resulting failure is starting from that possibility rather than from the value the connection is supposed to deliver.
claims.quote_verbatim: if we just make a thing and put it on the internet, then we have value
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: On-premises infrastructure persists for concrete reasons — data integrity, data privacy law and raw latency — rather than as conservatism, and the economics reverse with scale: renting makes sense early and makes progressively less sense as the workload grows.
claims.quote_verbatim: there may be reasons for data integrity, data privacy laws, just a pure speed about not wanting to have things somewhere where people would still want to run things on premises
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: A defensible rule for home automation is that the installation must never depend on an external service: if everything cannot be controlled locally while the house is offline, the design is wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: the home should never be dependent on external services
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: Telemetry leaving a home leaks occupancy whether or not that was the intent, so the security question is not only whether the data is protected in transit but what the pattern of the data reveals about the people generating it.
claims.quote_verbatim: that also means someone might be able to read when you're home or not
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Access control built on hosted integrations has two independent failure paths: the building's connection dropping, and a vendor pushing an update that silently breaks an existing integration. Both were answered by adding edge computing to keep state synchronised locally.
claims.quote_verbatim: what happens when the building's internet goes down or what happens when the vendor pushes an update to their turnstile software and it breaks the previous integration
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: Software running on rented infrastructure has known, measurable network characteristics; the same software deployed across customer premises does not, and that unpredictability is a different engineering problem rather than the same one at a smaller scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: the premises of running software in the cloud where we control the servers on Amazon and you know exactly how close they are or how slow they are. It's just a wild west
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: An outage is a payroll problem rather than an inconvenience once a shop's machines depend on the tool, which is why an operator who genuinely values the collaboration features — shared tool libraries across every machine in the shop — would still take the local option if given the choice.
claims.quote_verbatim: when it goes down, you know, I'm not a hobby anymore. I have a payroll. I've got machines to run
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: A substantial number of engineering companies still do not permit internet access on design workstations at all, which excludes hosted tooling by policy regardless of its technical merits.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of, you'd be surprised, a lot of engineering companies still do not allow internet on the desktop
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: The vendor's security argument is that a team works full time on protecting the stored files while almost nobody is doing the equivalent for an individual workstation, and that a breach is existential for the vendor in a way it is not for the customer.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've got a ton of people that spend every day trying to make sure that your files don't get broken into versus like how many guys at your workplace
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: The elastic model — spin up a virtual server on demand, scale it down again, pay only for consumption — is what let small companies do work that previously required buying a server and renting co-location space.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can spin it up or down. You just pay for what you use
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: The major infrastructure services are built for power users rather than beginners; the barrier to using them is learning them, not obtaining them, and the dozens of separate offerings are themselves part of the difficulty.
claims.quote_verbatim: these Amazon services are not easy to implement
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Amazon Moves In, Dave Says Run

claims.claim_text: Renting many machines for a few minutes each at well under a dollar apiece converts a slow batch tool into an interactive one, and that change in wall-clock time changes the workflow: a five-hour autorouting run competes with doing the layout by hand, while a one-minute run supports tweak-and-rerun iteration.
claims.quote_verbatim: i can buy multiple servers for a few minutes for less you know less than a dollar each and just run my problem really wide across tons of servers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Long FPGA and ASIC builds can be partitioned into chunks and run in parallel on disposable compute, which breaks the assumption that the only way to speed up hardware development is to buy a bigger workstation.
claims.quote_verbatim: are ways to accelerate those processes like design, development, test for FPGAs, for ASICs in the cloud. Partitioning those into smaller chunks
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Continuous integration platforms are dimensioned for software build times and software memory footprints; hardware tools with very large RAM requirements need custom runners on your own or rented machines, with the platform reduced to orchestration.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of the tools have ridiculous like RAM requirements and you just, the default machines just don't have that
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A browser front end to a remote tool is a remote display and nothing more, so the engineering problem is network latency to the data centre; where that latency is high the design size has to be capped because the view refreshes too slowly to work with.
claims.quote_verbatim: the browser is nothing more than a delivery window. At the end of the day, I call it a remote display
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Putting design software, IP and foundry access behind one portal is straightforward to state and close to impossible inside the traditional licensed ecosystem, because each of the three is separately gated — which is why the open flow had to be assembled rather than bought.
claims.quote_verbatim: implies that the end gate, all of it would exist in the cloud, in a, in a portal where someone can
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Buying a conventional chip means buying a datasheet with no way to verify the claim until parts are on a board; hosted access to the register-transfer source lets a customer run their own code against the actual design before silicon exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually, you know, get the ground truth, the RTL code of the data sheet and run code on that in the cloud before you get the chip back
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Machines big enough to host that kind of interactive evaluation cost roughly one to ten dollars an hour, which makes giving prospective customers hands-on access a bounded cost-of-sales line rather than an open-ended commitment.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're spinning up servers that are like a buck to 10 bucks a minute. Sorry, an hour
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Hosted evaluation is a distribution strategy as much as a technical one: reaching ten thousand prospects is impossible through a sales force unless each deal is worth a million dollars, and self-serve access is what makes the smaller deal viable.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to reach 10,000 people, you, you can't do that with a Salesforce of 10,000 people
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Storing the environment definition alongside the source — the prerequisites and toolchain install steps as a script in the repository — lets a hosted development environment reproduce the build machine on demand, up to throwing thirty-two cores at a compile.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like a script file that basically says, here's, you know, go install all of these prerequisites and then go install this tool chain. You store that with your file
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For a small service the hosting is no longer a meaningful line item — rented virtual server space is cheap enough that owning hardware is not a consideration.
claims.quote_verbatim: just buy server space from DigitalOcean
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: Shared hosting stops coping somewhere around a terabyte of monthly transfer, where the symptom is intermittent dropouts rather than an outright failure, and that is the threshold that historically forced a move to elastic hosting.
claims.quote_verbatim: now I'm doing almost one terabyte of data transfer per month
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The operational value of a hosted component for deployed hardware is fleet visibility and controlled rollout: how many units exist, how many are active, which firmware revision each is running, and the ability to stage a migration rather than push to everything at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: can look at all of the. Activated devices
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Over-the-air update is two problems, not one: the firmware needs hooks capable of rewriting itself, and a server component has to exist to drive it — and the second half is frequently outside the skill set of the person who built the device.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to have some kind of hooks in the firmware
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Standardising the factory programming and test station as a Linux computer — carrying a programmable supply, a programmer, a meter and network access in one box — is what lets test reports leave the line automatically rather than surviving as files on a factory PC.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a Linux computer itself. And so that is what lets it securely connect to the cloud and push out the test reports
claims.speaker: Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: Running the network server on the gateway is fine for bench testing but wrong for deployment, because multiple gateways all have to reach the same server — so the component that looked local turns out to be inherently central.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can put it on your gateway, but that's for testing
claims.speaker: Richard Ginus

claims.claim_text: The large infrastructure providers are pushing their reach all the way down to the sensor, because owning the last link is what lets the connection be billed by the byte.
claims.quote_verbatim: these cloud providers want to get their fingers into the last micro-inch
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Many companies commissioning connected products treat the hardware as a necessary evil and want only the resulting data, but somebody still has to own the firmware, the electrical and mechanical design, the radios and the security before any of that data reaches anywhere useful.
claims.quote_verbatim: they definitely don't want to get involved in the nuts and bolts of how to build a thing. They just want the data
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep163 (Upverter founders) records both founders under one machine speaker label; those claims carry speaker: null.

ep349's rule about home automation never depending on external services is spoken by the guest Jon Oxer in the passage window and is attributed to him; the adjacent privacy observation is the host's and is attributed accordingly.
ep258, ep650 and ep651 are flagged unreliable and label host questions with the guest's name; only material unambiguously the guest's own was used.

This bundle is unusually opinion-heavy. Running host sentiment about hosted tools — the slogan about somebody else's computer, predictions that a product would sink, and general dislike of connected consumer devices — was excluded as non-transferable, keeping only the arguments that carry a stated mechanism or consequence.
